{{legend0|#F48882|Republican hold}} {{legend0|#CA0120|Republican gain}} | title = [[Speaker of the United States House of Representatives|Speaker]] | before_election = [[Nancy Pelosi]] | before_party = Democratic Party (US) | after_election = [[John Boehner]] | after_party = Republican Party (US) }} The '''2010 United States House of Representatives elections''' were held on November 2, 2010, as part of the [[2010 United States elections|2010 midterm elections]] during President [[Barack Obama]]'s first term in office. Voters of the 50 [[U.S. state]]s chose 435 [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. Representatives]] to serve in the [[112th United States Congress]]. Also, voters of the U.S. territories, commonwealths and District of Columbia chose their [[Non-voting members of the United States House of Representatives|non-voting delegates]].The nonvoting delegates represent the District of Columbia; the territories of American Samoa, Guam and the Virgin Islands; and the commonwealths of the Northern Mariana Islands and Puerto Rico, ''see'' {{USC|48|16}}. They are all chosen biennially except for [[Resident Commissioner of Puerto Rico|Puerto Rico's delegate]], who is elected every four years and next faced reelection in 2012. [[United States Senate|U.S. Senate]] [[2010 United States Senate elections|elections]] and various state and local elections were held on the same date. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republicans]] regained control of the U.S. House they had lost in the [[2006 United States House of Representatives elections|2006 midterm election]], picking up a net total of 62 seats and erasing the gains [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrats]] made in 2006 and [[2008 United States House of Representatives elections|2008]]. Although the sitting president's party usually loses seats in a midterm election, the 2010 election resulted in the highest losses by a party in a House midterm election since [[1938 United States House of Representatives elections|1938]],{{cite web | url=http://www2.nationaljournal.com/gop-projected-to-take-over-house-20101102 | title=Boehner Must Navigate Around Senate, Obama – And Tea Party | work=[[National Journal]] | date=November 3, 2010 | access-date=November 4, 2010 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101104210009/http://nationaljournal.com/gop-projected-to-take-over-house-20101102 | archive-date=November 4, 2010 | df=mdy-all }}{{cite web | url=http://nationaljournal.com/columns/political-connections/a-heartland-headache-for-dems-20101104 | title=Heartland Headache | work=National Journal | date=November 4, 2010 | access-date=November 24, 2010 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101125102409/http://nationaljournal.com/columns/political-connections/a-heartland-headache-for-dems-20101104 | archive-date=November 25, 2010 | df=mdy-all }} as well as the largest House swing since [[1948 United States House of Representatives elections|1948]].{{cite news | url=http://www.cnn.com/2010/POLITICS/11/03/election.house/ | title=Republicans capture control of House | publisher=CNN | date=November 3, 2010 | access-date=April 9, 2014}} In total, 52 House Democrats were defeated, including 36 freshman and sophomore representatives. Republicans made their largest gain in House seats since 1938.[http://www.commentarymagazine.com/2010/11/10/the-2010-midterm-election-in-perspective/ The 2010 Midterm Election in Perspective] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120119194747/http://www.commentarymagazine.com/2010/11/10/the-2010-midterm-election-in-perspective/ |date=January 19, 2012 }} November 10, 2010. Commentary. Three Democratic committee chairmen were defeated: transportation chairman [[Jim Oberstar]] of Minnesota, armed services chairman [[Ike Skelton]] of Missouri, and budget chairman [[John Spratt]] of South Carolina. Democrats made three pick-ups, winning an open seat in Delaware and defeating Republican incumbents in Hawaii and Louisiana.{{efn|Hawaii Republican [[Charles Djou]] was elected in a [[2010 Hawaii's 1st congressional district special election|special election]].}} The heavy Democratic Party losses in 2010 were attributed to anger at President Obama, opposition to the [[Affordable Care Act]] and [[American Recovery and Reinvestment Act]], large budget deficits, and the weak economy.{{cite web | url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/2010-11-02/republicans-approach-biggest-house-midterm-win-in-seven-decades.html | title=Democrats Face Biggest House Midterm Defeat in Years | author=Catherine Dodge and Lisa Lerer | publisher=Bloomberg | date=November 2, 2010 | access-date=March 11, 2014}}{{cite news | url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/special/politics/2010-midterm-analysis/ | title=Midterms 2010: What you need to know | newspaper=Washington Post | access-date=March 11, 2014}}{{cite magazine | url=https://swampland.time.com/2010/11/02/mixed-results-on-the-health-reform-referendum/ | title=Mixed Results on the Health Reform Referendum | author=Kate Pickert | magazine=TIME | date=November 2, 2010 | access-date=March 11, 2014}} This is the last election in which Democrats won a seat in [[Arkansas's congressional districts|Arkansas]], and the last in which Republicans won more than one [[Maryland's congressional districts|seat in Maryland]], as well as [[New Hampshire's congressional districts|both seats in New Hampshire]]. ==Background== [[File:Boehner for Speaker Bumper Sticker.jpg|260px|thumb|right|An anti-Pelosi "Boehner for Speaker" bumper sticker on a car window.]] Following the [[2006 United States House of Representatives elections|2006 elections]], Democrats took control of the House as well as the Senate. In the [[2008 United States House of Representatives elections|2008 elections]], which coincided with Democrat [[Barack Obama]]'s [[2008 United States presidential election|victory]] over Republican [[John McCain]] for the [[President of the United States|presidency]], Democrats increased their majorities in both chambers. Of the 435 congressional districts, 242 were carried by Obama, while 193 voted for McCain. Of the districts Obama won, 34 elected a Republican to the House, while 49 of the districts McCain won elected a Democrat.{{cite web | url=http://innovation.cq.com/atlas/district_08?referrer=tout | title=CQ Politics {{pipe}} Presidential and House election 08 results by congressional district | publisher=Innovation.cq.com | access-date=July 28, 2009 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110708200855/http://innovation.cq.com/atlas/district_08?referrer=tout | archive-date=July 8, 2011 | df=mdy-all }} ===Republican gains=== The Republicans' 63-seat pickup in the House to take control of that chamber, as well as their gain of six Senate seats, signified a dramatic rollback of recent Democratic gains. In the election, Republicans won their greatest number of House seats since 1946.{{cite web|url=http://www.nationalaffairs.com/publications/detail/after-the-wave |title=After the Wave > Publications > |work=National Affairs |date=November 2, 2010 |access-date=March 7, 2012}} This has been attributed to the continued economic recession, as well as President Obama's controversial [[American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009|stimulus]] and [[Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act|health care reform]] bills. Republicans also took control of 29 of the 50 state governorships and gained 690 seats in state legislatures, to hold their greatest number since the 1928 elections.{{cite web |last=Drake |first=Bruce |url=http://www.politicsdaily.com/2010/11/03/republicans-score-big-in-the-states-and-win-leg-up-on-redistrict/ |title=Republicans Score Big in the States and Win Leg Up on Redistricting |publisher=Politicsdaily.com |access-date=March 7, 2012 |archive-date=February 2, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120202032104/http://www.politicsdaily.com/2010/11/03/republicans-score-big-in-the-states-and-win-leg-up-on-redistrict/ |url-status=dead }} Republicans also made historic gains in [[State legislature (United States)|state legislatures]], adding more than 675 state legislative seats, by far surpassing their state-legislative gains in 1994.[http://www.ncsl.org/research/elections-and-campaigns/statevote-2010.aspx Map of Post 2010 Election Partisan Composition of State Legislatures: Republicans Make Historic Gains], [[National Conference of State Legislatures]].Dan Balz, [https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2010/11/13/AR2010111302389.html The GOP takeover in the states], ''Washington Post'' (November 13, 2010). Republicans gained control of dozens of state legislative chambers, and took control of "seven more legislatures outright than they did after 1994 and the most since 1952." Republicans picked up control of the [[Alabama Legislature]] for the first time since [[Reconstruction era in the United States|Reconstruction]]; control of the [[North Carolina Senate]] for the first time since 1870; and control of the [[Minnesota Senate]] for the first time since the state returned to partisan elections in 1974. The [[Great Lakes region]], which until then had recently favored the Democratic Party, went strongly Republican. In California and the [[Pacific Northwest]], however, the Democrats retained the upper hand.Paul R Abramson, John H Aldrich and David W Rohde, ''Change and Continuity in the 2008 and 2010 Elections'' (2011) The biggest change in 2010 occurred in the [[Southern United States]], which had previously been roughly evenly split between Democrats and Republicans for everything except for president. Just one white Democrat from the Deep South won reelection to the US House in 2010. Prior to 2010, many white conservative southerners had voted Republican for president, but Democratic for other offices.{{Cite news |title=The long goodbye |url=https://www.economist.com/united-states/2010/11/11/the-long-goodbye |access-date=2024-07-10 |work=The Economist |issn=0013-0613}} == Results summary == === Federal === {| style="width:60%; text-align:center" |- | colspan=3 style="text-align:center" | {{Down-arrow|alt=Midpoint}} |- | style="background:{{party color|Republican Party (US)}}; width:55.63%; color:#fff;" | '''242''' | style="background:{{party color|Democratic Party (US)}}; width:44.37%; color:#fff;" | '''193''' |- | Republican | Democratic |} {| class=wikitable style="text-align:center" ! rowspan=2 colspan=2 | Parties (and Independents) ! colspan=4 | Seats ! colspan=3 | Popular vote |- style="background:#e9e9e9" !
